#5540. TEN Holdings Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD), through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., the technology company behind TEN, a Digital Experience Platform that powers the next generation of enterprise digital engagement, today announced its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Third quarter revenue increased 17.9% year over year to $640,000, as we completed customer engagements that had been initiated in prior periods and added revenue from new customers," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings. "Our performance reflects continued demand for our digital engagement solutions and our ability to serve both existing and new customers. As we look ahead, our focus remains on expanding recurring revenue, strengthening our technology platform, and accelerating our transition toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model."

"Our third-quarter results reflect two significant expenses that we consider non-recurring: a $1.8 million write-off of previously capitalized service contracts and approximately $0.5 million in legal expenses. Excluding these items, our underlying selling, general and administrative expenses declined compared to the same period last year, reflecting the progress we have made in improving operational efficiency. Over the past 12 months, we have reduced our annual operating cost structure by approximately $2.5 million through strategic cost reductions, process improvements, and the integration of AI-driven tools to streamline engineering and accelerate product development. With these efficiencies largely implemented and a leaner operating structure in place, we are now shifting our focus toward accelerating revenue growth, expanding customer relationships, and scaling TEN, our new platform."

"We also made significant progress in strengthening our balance sheet, reducing short-term related-party borrowings from $4.6 million at the beginning of the year to approximately $0.1 million as of September 30, 2026. Total liabilities declined by approximately 74%, from $7.7 million at year-end 2025 to $2.0 million, reflecting our continued efforts to simplify our capital structure and improve our financial position."

"One of our most significant milestones this year was the launch of TEN, our next-generation Digital Experience Platform, whose development was accelerated by investments made possible through the proceeds of our June common stock offering, consistent with our previously communicated commitment to product development. TEN represents an important step in our evolution toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model, bringing together the tools organizations need to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences within a unified platform.

At launch, TEN provides enterprises with a self-service solution for webinars, virtual events, and continuing education programs, with the capacity to support up to 50,000 concurrent attendees. Building on our longstanding relationships with enterprise customers, many of whom rely on our technology for recurring digital engagement initiatives, we see a meaningful opportunity to transition these relationships toward subscription-based arrangements. We believe this approach will deliver greater flexibility and value to our customers while creating a more predictable and recurring revenue stream for TEN Holdings."

"Looking ahead, we are focused on three priorities: continuing the transition of our business from a managed services provider to a SaaS company, investing in TEN so that it remains competitive, and executing an acquisition strategy aimed at accretive businesses that add revenue and EBITDA, products our sales team can scale, and technology that complements our own. With TEN now in the market, a leaner cost structure, and a simplified balance sheet, we believe TEN Holdings is positioned to build a more scalable, recurring revenue business and create long-term value for our shareholders."

#5539. NRMLA asks Congress to restore HUD housing counseling funds

NRMLA asked congressional appropriators to restore rescinded HUD housing counseling funds tied to the HECM process. The group said mandatory third-party counseling is required to legally close federally insured reverse mortgages.  AI Summary

The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) is urging Congress to restore funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)’s housing counseling program, warning that cuts could disrupt the origination of federally insured reverse mortgages.

In a Nov. 2 letter to congressional appropriations leaders, NRMLA President Steve Irwin raised concerns about the presidential pocket rescission of appropriated funds for HUD’s housing counseling program, specifically the funding that supports the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) program.

NRMLA said independent, third-party counseling is a statutory requirement for every prospective HECM borrower. Under Section 255 of the National Housing Act, borrowers must receive counseling from a HUD-approved agency before a loan can close.

A counseling certificate issued by a certified counselor is required for a HECM loan to be legally closed, the trade group said.

The association also emphasized that lenders cannot pay for a borrower’s counseling session, direct borrowers to a particular counseling agency or use an agency affiliated with the lender. These restrictions are intended to ensure seniors receive objective information about reverse mortgage costs, obligations and alternatives.

Because lenders are prohibited from funding or steering the counseling process, NRMLA said federal appropriations are essential to maintaining the independent counseling infrastructure required for HECM originations.

Without the funding, the association warned, mandatory counseling could become less accessible and affordable for seniors, potentially creating obstacles to loan closings and limiting access to the federally insured reverse mortgage program.

The HECM program allows eligible older homeowners to access their home equity to support aging in place and improve their financial security. Irwin asked congressional leaders to take action to restore the funds, arguing that the funding is necessary to preserve the program as a housing finance option for seniors.

“We respectfully urge you to take the necessary action to restore the appropriated HUD housing counseling funds so that eligible seniors may continue to benefit from the HECM program,” he wrote.

The association represents more than 300 member companies and more than 2,000 member delegates. Its members originate more than 90% of reverse mortgages, according to the letter.

#5538. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5536. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5534. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5533. Blend posts smaller Q3 loss, warns of steeper mortgage revenue drop ahead

Blend Labs reported Q3 revenue of $32.9 million, up 1% year over year, and cut its GAAP operating loss to $2.6 million from $5.3 million. Mortgage suite revenue slipped 2% as funded loans on the platform fell 4% to 194,000 and value per loan reached $81.   AI Summary

Blend Labs narrowed its loss in the third quarter and logged its strongest period of sales in more than three years, even as rising mortgage rates pressured loan volumes and its core mortgage suite revenue declined.

Total revenue in the third quarter was $32.9 million, up 1% from the same period in 2025, the company reported Thursday. GAAP operating loss was $2.6 million, an improvement from a $5.3 million loss a year earlier.

“The market got harder, but we’re moving faster than ever,” Nima Ghamsari, co-founder and head of Blend, told analysts on an earnings call. “When we spoke in August, mortgage rates were about 6.8%. After the Fed raised rates in September, they hit a high of north of 7.5%. And as you can expect, applications dropped with them — purchase and refinance both.”

Blend closed 26 new deals and expansions during the quarter. In dollar terms, the company said, these moves represented more than twice the combined value of its first- and second-quarter deals.

Churn notices in the quarter represented about $2 million of annual revenue, an improvement from roughly $3 million in the second quarter. Based on a lighter churn environment in the first quarter and subsequent improvement, Blend said year-to-date gross revenue retention is in the mid-90% range.

“Three takeaways for today: One, We had our best sales quarter in more than three years; two, Autopilot went from six customers to 10 and the pipeline behind it is now big enough to size and growing; three, next year the market may not help us. Converting Autopilot pipeline is how we’re going to grow,” Ghamsari said.

Revenue from Blend’s mortgage suite totaled $17.4 million in the third quarter, down 2% year over year. The platform handled 194,000 funded mortgages, a 4% decline from the same period last year, and economic value per funded loan was $81.

In a compressed market, lenders are relying on Blend’s Rapid Mortgage and Rapid Home Equity solutions to lower per-loan costs and accelerate consumer-facing processes “when every basis point counts,” Ghamsari said.

For the fourth quarter, Blend guided total revenue to a range of $27.7 million to $29.7 million, a decline of about 8% to 15% year over year. Mortgage suite revenue is expected to fall 23% to 28% from the prior-year period, reflecting lower industry volumes and mix shifts.

Executives said potential fourth-quarter deals could contribute about $5 million in incremental revenue in 2027 as implementations go live. “Next year the market may not help us,” Ghamsari said.

Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote that Blend is “executing on what it can control against a weak mortgage market” and that “early traction with budding AI products (Autopilot) is encouraging.”

“We continue to think upside in the shares will be capped until there is visibility into a more meaningful and sustained acceleration in revenue growth (thus driving more scaled profitability), which the weak mortgage backdrop pushes out,” the analysts wrote.

Blend ended the quarter with $44.2 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, and no debt.

#5531. NAR President Kevin Brown warns of outside forces threatening real estate marketplace

Outgoing NAR President Kevin Brown defended the MLS model as central to transparency and competition while warning that outside interests could seek more control of the marketplace. He also addressed NAR reforms, legislative priorities and member accountability ahead of a leadership transition.  AI Summary

As his term as president of the National Association of Realtors (NAR) comes to a close, Kevin Brown is warning real estate professionals that outside forces seeking greater control of the industry could threaten the transparency and competition that are the backbone of the current real estate marketplace.

In remarks prepared for NAR NXT in New Orleans this week, Brown drew parallels between the forces that contributed to the 2008 housing crisis and those he believes are now attempting to reshape how real estate is bought and sold.

“Today, outside forces have once again entered our industry, and this time around it is our marketplace instead of our financial system, motivated by profits, control and market share,” Brown said.

He did not identify the companies or organizations he was referring to, but his comments come as the industry debates the future of listing distribution, broker control of listing data and the role of multiple listing services (MLSs).

Brown said he believes the MLS system remains essential to maintaining competition and giving buyers and sellers access to comprehensive property information.

“America is home to the fairest, most accessible and transparent real estate market in the world,” Brown said. “That is because of a pro-competitive foundation that provides the broadest, most reliable view of the market, anchored in the MLS system.”

Perhaps in a nod to the increase in private listings, he emphasized that consumer choice depends not only on the ability to make decisions but also on access to the information needed to make them.

“A fair and transparent marketplace gives homebuyers and sellers both choice and clarity — the freedom to choose and the information to understand the consequences of that choice,” he said.

According to Brown, NAR is working with MLSs, associations and industry leaders to address marketplace concerns while advocating for the MLS system in Washington.

He also urged members to take a more active role in defending the existing marketplace. “Be prepared to support and defend a marketplace that doesn’t just benefit a select few, but a marketplace that serves us all — the consumer, the industry and Realtors,” Brown said.

When it comes to the association, Brown acknowledged shortcomings. “If NAR wants to lead change, we must be willing to change ourselves,” Brown said. “We cannot wait for outside forces to set our agenda or determine our direction.”

Brown pointed to organizational changes this year, including staff reductions, streamlined governance and a renewed focus on member services. These changes are part of NAR’s three-year strategic plan, which focuses on rebuilding the member experience and modernizing the association.

“That is why we have rightsized our staff, streamlined our governance structure and sharpened our focus,” he said. “But the real test is not whether we created a plan. It is whether that plan helps you get to your next transaction, better serve your clients and move our industry forward.”

Brown also strongly addressed criticism of NAR, acknowledging the association’s shortcomings while challenging critics to provide accurate information. “Accountability starts with being honest about where NAR has fallen short, what must change and whether we are delivering value for you,” Brown said.

But Brown also took aim at what he characterized as sensationalized coverage of the association. “For some, reporting on NAR’s progress is not a profitable story. Sensationalism sells,” Brown said. “We are not interested in fueling miscommunication and half-truths to boost views, profits or egos.”

Brown maintained that criticism is necessary but said it must be grounded in facts. “We respect our critics,” he said. “Honest criticism makes us better and helps hold us accountable.”

Brown also highlighted NAR’s legislative efforts, including passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

“It took Realtors to get it across the finish line,” Brown said. He also pointed to efforts to modernize credit scoring and help delinquent veteran homeowners avoid foreclosure.

As Brown prepares to hand over the presidency to Florida’s Christine Hansen, he acknowledged that the association still has work to do. “NAR is not perfect and our work is not finished,” he said.

And while he warns that criticism of the association should be based on facts, he insists that members continue to hold NAR accountable. “Keep asking us the hard questions,” Brown said. “Keep holding us responsible for clear communication and meaningful results.”

#5530. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5529. Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B

Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a deal valued at $5.3 billion.

The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.

Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.

The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.

Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.

Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.

According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team.

Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.

The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.

Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.

Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.

#5527. Elizabeth Warren expected to lead Senate banking committee in January

Elizabeth Warren is expected to chair the Senate banking committee in January after Democrats flipped Congress. The role would expand her investigative authority and could increase scrutiny of banks, lenders, private equity and crypto, alongside oversight of CFPB changes.   AI Summary

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to become chair of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs when Democrats take control of Congress in January, giving the Massachusetts Democrat expanded authority to investigate financial institutions and advance legislation affecting the sector.

The move is expected as a result of this week’s midterm elections, which saw both the Senate and House of Representatives flip from Republican to Democratic majorities.

Several outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and Reuters, anticipate that Warren is lined up for the role, even though other senators could theoretically rank ahead of her for the chairmanship.

The transition would give Warren, who is currently a ranking member of the legislative committee, more staff and subpoena powers, potentially increasing scrutiny of major banks, consumer lenders, private equity firms and cryptocurrency companies.

Warren, who would replace current Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.), is also expected to examine the Trump administration’s mass firings of financial regulatory employees and potential conflicts of interest involving companies with ties to the president.

Warren has built her political career around financial regulation and consumer protection. A former Harvard University law professor and bankruptcy expert, she became involved in developing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in the wake of the great financial crisis under President Barack Obama before winning a Senate seat in 2012.

Her expected chairmanship comes as the CFPB faces significant operational challenges and restructuring under the Trump administration, a move that she has publicly criticized.

The administration, meanwhile, has argued that the CFPB over-regulates consumer lenders and has been used to target political opponents and disfavored industries, going so far as to scale back enforcements this year.

The CFPB has undergone a leadership shuffle as a result of the administration’s efforts to scale back the agency’s power. In September, the committee advanced the nomination of Brian Johnson, Trump’s newest nominee to become director of the bureau, a move that Warren opposed.

#5526. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

LAS VEGAS, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At the recently concluded AAPEX 2026, more than 45,000 professionals from 128 countries and regions and over 2,500 exhibitors gathered in Las Vegas, a clear sign of sourcing demand across the global automotive aftermarket. At the same time, a long-standing industry challenge has become harder to ignore: as vehicle model counts keep climbing and model refresh cycles shorten, global repair networks are commonly facing difficulties in parts data matching, fragmented supply sources, low quotation efficiency, and insufficient repair technical capabilities.

In response to these bottlenecks, Li Li, CEO of International Business at CassTime, introduced an AI-driven "T+D Solution" at the 2026 CassTime Partner Conference. T refers to Digital Trade, which connects supply with overseas procurement demand through the CassChoice platform; D refers to an intelligent localized service platform, which uses PartGrid to bring parts matching, repair support, and insurance claims assessment capabilities to local markets. The solution has already been put into practical operation in markets such as Saudi Arabia.

Industry Bottlenecks: Data Matching and Repair Capability Are Global Challenges

Li Li noted that channel and market-access conditions vary significantly across regions: the Middle East has many new vehicle models and a growing number of supply channels; Brazil has a complex channel and market-access system; Central Asia's supply channels are being restructured; and North America has mature certification and channel requirements for branded parts. The common challenges are concentrated in four areas: data matching, supply stability, quotation and delivery efficiency, and local repair service capability. Insufficient data leads to matching difficulties, fragmented demand leads to unstable supply, and local repair capabilities are difficult to build up quickly.

"After decades of development, the automotive aftermarket has formed a complete supply chain system, and CassTime has also built a digital system covering the entire value chain," Li Li said. "We hope to translate proven digital practices into a holistic solution that can be implemented overseas, covering both parts and repair services."

Li Li emphasized that China's auto parts industry has been tempered through intense competition and has long built a comprehensive domestic supply chain. In particular, its parts SKU coverage for Chinese-brand vehicles is especially complete: Chinese vehicle models have a large installed base and rapid update and iteration cycles. Leveraging deep accumulation in the local market, CassTime has formed the industry's most complete coverage in parts data, VIN decoding, and repair cases for Chinese-brand vehicles. This is also the foundation of the T+D Solution. Supported by this most complete Chinese-brand vehicle SKU database, wherever Chinese-brand vehicles go in the world, CassTime can bring along the parts supply and repair experience already proven in China, enabling overseas partners to share the best practices of China's supply chain.

CassChoice: Digital Trade to Solve Supply-Demand Matching Challenges

In traditional procurement scenarios, when a customer submits demand for hundreds of thousands of SKUs, it usually requires manual order splitting, separate inquiries to multiple suppliers, quotation consolidation, and delivery in batchesâa long and inefficient process. The CassChoice system can automatically break down demand, generate batch quotations, track order status, and output reports. The relevant data can also be used for demand tracking and analysisâa direct manifestation of using AI and digital tools to solve "difficult data matching and fragmented supply."

According to CassTime, its overseas platform has accumulated more than 5 million SKUsâwith particularly complete SKU data for Chinese-brand vehiclesâand can generate quotes in seconds for more than 10,000 SKUs. On the supply side, CassChoice connects factories, brands, and distributors, helping overseas customers complete sourcing, procurement, and local delivery, and efficiently matching fragmented supply with fragmented demand on a digital platform.

PartGrid: AI Agents to Fill Local Repair Capability Gaps

To address matching challenges caused by the large number and rapid updates of vehicle models, PartGrid integrates CassTime's VIN decoding system to help local partners achieve precise matching just as they would in China, reducing error rates. Multilingual communication is handled by AI, enabling barrier-free interaction. The platform can use formats such as WhatsApp Chatbot to connect with local users, adapting to the usage habits of small repair businesses and end users.

Beyond parts circulation, PartGrid also provides three AI agent service capabilities: an AI Repair Master, which synchronizes accumulated repair data and cases to local markets to help solve technical difficulties, especially overseas repair of Chinese vehicle models; an insurance claims assessment agent, which combines real-time fault analysis, parts matching information, and labor-hour estimation to support efficient implementation of insurance business; and an AI Seller, which provides accurate and timely quotations around the clock. Together, these three capabilities form a localized service loop of "parts + repair + insurance," directly addressing the industry bottleneck of "repair capability falling behind."

The two parties began their cooperation with online access in claims scenarios: through PartGrid, the partner's platform connects local car owners, workshops, and the supply chain to enable digital tracking and management of the process; through CassChoice, it connects supply, opening up the parts value chain from source to end user.

On this basis, the cooperation has three expansion directions: extending application scenarios from claims to more end-user demand; as workshops adoption and business volume grow, more local suppliers join the platform; and upstream factories, brands, and distributors connecting to supply.

At present, CassTime has advanced implementation in the Middle East and is extending the mature model to Central Asia, South America, and other regions, accelerating the construction of a global parts service network. #5524. Massachusetts AG issues rule on shared appreciation mortgages, NCLC calls for broader protections

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, a dual-lien structure that ties repayment to home price appreciation. The regulation clarifies when nonprofit lenders are shielded from consumer protection claims and requires stronger disclosures, including maximum potential repayment amounts. Stemming from a 2024 law that granted broad liability waivers to nonprofit SAMs such as BlueHub, the rule follows litigation alleging the products function as high-cost, subprime-style loans that can strip home equity.   AI Summary

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, adding disclosure and consumer protection requirements for a niche home equity product that has faced recent scrutiny.

The rule, effective Nov. 6, clarifies when nonprofit shared appreciation mortgage (SAM) lenders are shielded from state consumer protection claims and sets new notice standards, including prominent disclosure of the maximum amount borrowers may have to repay, according to an announcement from the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC).

The regulation stems from a provision in the state’s economic development bill, passed in November 2024. That statute carved out a broad waiver of liability under Massachusetts consumer protection laws for certain nonprofit SAMs, including loans originated by BlueHub Capital. Advocates say the legislative change created a “dangerous loophole” that exposed distressed homeowners to complex and costly loan structures with limited recourse.

Under the BlueHub-style model, borrowers typically receive a fixed-rate first mortgage alongside a second lien tied to future home price appreciation. The SAM second lien requires the homeowner to share a portion of any increase in property value with the lender upon sale, transfer or refinance. Because the payoff amount is variable and not set in dollars at origination, borrowers can face unexpectedly large balloon payments when they attempt to exit the loan.

NCLC noted that the risks of these structures have been highlighted in Humes v. BlueHub Capital Inc., a Massachusetts class-action lawsuit alleging SAMs embed hidden, subprime-level costs that can strip significant equity and accelerate home loss. The court found BlueHub liable for violating multiple state lending laws and recently certified the class to move forward, according to NCLC.

“While presented as a lifeline, shared appreciation mortgages often become a trap,” Andrea Bopp Stark, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said in a statement. “The AG’s final rule protects people from BlueHub’s loan model and similar products, but Massachusetts must go further to prevent harm from more common home equity theft loan products, including Home Equity Investment Loans.”

The AG’s new rule does not eliminate SAMs but seeks to ensure that nonprofit and other lenders using these instruments do so transparently and within defined consumer protection boundaries.

The regulation spells out the limited circumstances in which a SAM lender can be insulated from claims under Massachusetts consumer protection law and establishes a framework for robust disclosures, including clear presentation of the maximum possible repayment obligation.

While praising the change, NCLC argues that the rule does not reach a far enough to impact a growing category of products — home equity investments (HEIs). These provide upfront cash to a homeowner in exchange for a share of the future home price appreciation. NCLC characterized these arrangements as high risk for borrowers, as the actual amount owed depends on home price growth and triggers large, lump-sum obligations.

A representative at the AG’s office did not immediately respond to HousingWire‘s request for comment on the changes.

Massachusetts AG Andrea Joy Campbell has already challenged one HEI provider, Hometap. The state alleges consumer protection violations tied to HEI structures. But NCLC noted that the latest rulemaking in Massachusetts does not specifically regulate HEI products.

“The new rules provide important safeguards and requirements for SAMs, and stronger and broader rules are needed to address the high-risk HEI loans that are now targeting Massachusetts homeowners,” Bopp Stark said.

Consumers in other parts of the country have challenged HEI providers in court. Last year, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a 2023 judgment from a district court in Washington state, ruling that Unison‘s HEI product amounted to a reverse mortgage under state law.

In August, HEI provider Unlock settled with the Office of the Minnesota Attorney General over allegations that the company’s home equity agreements (HEAs) were mortgage loans that violated state usury caps, disclosure rules and licensing requirements.

Companies say they are supportive of regulatory efforts, pointing to a legal framework passed earlier this year in Illinois that could serve as model at the national level. At the Mortgage Bankers Association‘s Annual Convention & Expo last month, executives at Point told HousingWire they believe universal regulations are coming.

“We believe that these companies are going to be regulated,” said Dan McPheeters, Point’s head of business development and partnerships. “The practical effect is, it’s difficult to comply with [mortgage regulations] for a product that doesn’t have a monthly payment, that isn’t self-amortizing. … That said, as long as you address those tactical issues, this should be regulated.”

The NCLC urges additional state action to close what they see as remaining gaps in oversight of shared appreciation equity-based mortgage products. Their recommendations include:

#5523. Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features

Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million.

The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX Agent Cloud, a service that artificial intelligence agents can use to store their data. Dropbox is also adding new AI productivity features to its flagship file sharing platform.

Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris Data offers an object storage service that runs across multiple public clouds. The company says that it enables applications to read and write several times faster than competing offerings. Furthermore, the service includes several features designed to optimize AI workloads.

AI agents often run in sandboxes that include, among other resources, the data they need to carry out their work. Loading data into a sandbox can be a relatively time-consuming process, which slows agent performance. Tigris Data offers a feature called bucket forms that speeds up the workflow. Furthermore, it prevents agents from modifying information that is used by other workloads.

Tigris Data’s service monitors the locations from which agents access records. When it detects a new location, it moves a copy of the records to a nearby server in order to reduce latency. The service caches the most frequently used files on high-speed storage infrastructure to further reduce access times.

Dropbox said Tigris Data will support its push into the AI infrastructure market. The company debuted its first entry into that product category, DBX Agent Cloud, in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Like Tigris Data’s service, it’s an S3-compatible object storage offering optimized for AI agents.

The storage stalwart plans to add a file system capability further down the line. Object storage is best suited for unstructured datasets, while file systems are used to store records that are organized into folders. Dropbox plans to release the technology alongside “content processing capabilities.” The company says that those features will make it easier for AI models to process information kept in DBX Agent Cloud.

The offering is rolling out alongside a major overhaul of Dropbox’s flagship file sharing platform. An enhanced search bar will enable users to look for images by entering a description of the file they seek.

Furthermore, Dropbox can now respond to questions about a file by generating a natural language summary. A worker could, for example, request an overview of the changes that colleagues have made to an important folder over the past week.

Dropbox can not only edit questions about files but also edit them. The company says that users can have the built-in AI models change a file’s format, move it to a different folder or combine it with other records into a PDF document. Several other actions are supported as well. Users can mix and match actions into multistep workflows.

The new AI productivity features are initially available to customers in the U.S., the U.K. and Australia with Standard and Advanced subscriptions. Dropbox plans to expand access next year.

#5522. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

Built on a microcontroller-based, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) architecture, the series replaces discrete circuit breakers, solid state relays and system monitors with one intelligent unit that switches, protects and reports on up to 16 electrical loads.

#5519. How a new Pulte Florida agrihood makes conservation a buyer desire

PulteGroup is developing The Grow, a 1,200-acre agrihood east of Orlando planned for about 2,200 homes anchored by a 9-acre working farm. Plans leave just over half the site undeveloped, positioning the project as a growth and conservation case study.  AI Summary

For years, Central Florida’s exploding population growth and rapidly expanding suburban sprawl have clashed with local efforts to protect the region’s dwindling green space and undeveloped land. PulteGroup’s new 1,200-acre community on Orlando’s eastern edge aims to balance these seemingly contradictory interests.

The community is called The Grow. Once undeveloped, rural land, the property is set to begin morphing into a roughly 2,200-home “agrihood” centered around a 9-acre working farm. In keeping with its conservation focus, the plan calls for reserving just over half of the site from development, including wetlands, conservation areas and shared green space.

The Grow offers a potential case study in balancing growth and conservation, a tension deeply felt in Central Florida and many other high-growth Sun Belt markets. Between 2000 and 2025, the Orlando metro area’s population grew nearly 80%, from 1.64 million to 2.95 million.

That growth reshaped once-rural communities on the region’s edges, replacing undeveloped land with new subdivisions, apartments and shopping centers. Many long-time Sunshine State residents now lament the loss of “Old Florida,” marked by a landscape of open land, working ranches and orange groves that are now developed.

When Pulte, the sole homebuilder at The Grow, purchased the community’s lots in 2023, it set out to build a premier community that responded to these tensions.

“One of our biggest selling features is the openness of the community and how much greenery we left. Everywhere you look, you’re surrounded by trees,” Patrick McNamara, a Sales Manager at Pulte, told HousingWire TBD.

However, the true distinguisher between The Grow and other local communities will be its working farm, a rare amenity that carries the conservation theme beyond protecting land to putting it to use.

For Pulte, which held a grand opening for the community in late September, the farm and the extensive conservation space give the builder a way to stand out to prospective homebuyers, a crucial edge considering the challenging sales environment homebuilders are facing.

The working farm is central to the community’s agrihood concept – providing fresh, sustainably grown produce. Residents will support it by buying products, volunteering and joining educational activities.

McNamara argued that the farm creates a direct connection between residents and their food. A professional third-party company will manage the farm, but residents and families will be allowed to volunteer and then buy the finished produce at a resident-only general store that will serve as an anchor for The Grow’s commercial and retail street.

The development will include two other farms: a small demonstration farm, covering about an eighth of an acre, and a separate community farm where homeowners can practice what they learn.

These smaller farms will serve as an educational, hands-on amenity for families, where residents can learn each stage of growing produce and then put what they learn into practice. An existing program, “Seed the Table,” will allow residents to plant crops, watch them grow and eat what they produced.

The farmers will also work with the lifestyle director to hold chef-led cooking classes at the community’s gathering barn, and will host seasonal celebrations and festivals that bring homeowners together.

Beyond conservation and sustainability, the farm is meant to build community, encourage learning and offer a unique lifestyle.

The Grow, which features homes from the low $400s to the high $800s, isn’t immune to the macro-level sales pressures impacting the local and national housing market. McNamara concedes that his team has to leverage generous incentives like mortgage rate buydowns to finish sales.

However, he also confirmed that The Grow has sold more than 100 homes since opening pre-sales about six months ago, and that prospective buyers have been anticipating the community’s opening for years.

The agrihood concept is the hook that draws buyers in.

“The farm is a big draw,” McNamara said. “I think the agrihood is what’s bringing people in, but what’s getting them to buy is once they see everything else that comes with it.”

In addition to the working farm and conservation space, The Grow will feature a main street with about 170,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, envisioned as a high-end retail and dining corridor that can work as a visitor magnet.

Other features include an indoor event and social space, an outdoor green space with a community pizza oven, a dedicated dog park, walking and nature trails, playgrounds and other resident-only amenities like a clubhouse, a gym and a pool.

“[Buyers] are shocked to find out that this isn’t a little farm community. This is a high-end resort neighborhood.”

The community’s preservation of nature is another big selling point. While many newly built communities lack mature trees and vegetation, The Grow’s preservation space means that residents can live alongside nature from day one.

“It’s really about getting immersed in nature, and that’s really hard to find in new construction,” McNamara said. “Homebuilders typically buy a piece of land and clear it out, start from scratch, and then plant a lot of trees. But you’ve got another 30 years until you can really enjoy the shade from it. In this neighborhood, we’ve left hundreds of 100-year-old oaks all throughout the community. We’ve made them focal points.”

“One of the big draws is the lifestyle and the outdoor feeling that you’re going to have in this community,” he added

#5518. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5516. Atomicwork launches certified AI coworker marketplace for enterprise IT and security

Information technology service management startup Atomicwork Inc. today announced the launch of an Artificial Intelligence Coworker Marketplace that will give enterprise IT and security teams access to prebuilt, certified AI coworkers that can work alongside employees.

The company said these agentic AI coworkers include verified roles and capabilities across cloud infrastructure, access management, security and device operations.

“Most AI-native ITSM vendors today don’t have much to show for their agents’ effectiveness — a listing means ‘this agent works,’ not ‘this AI Agent has real, verified coverage of the systems it needs to touch and has been tested and fine-tuned using real-world enterprise use cases,’ which has made enterprises wary of agentic claims,” co-founder and Chief Executive Vijay Rayapati told SiliconANGLE.

Founded in 2022, Atomicwork began with the premise that information technology and security teams face challenging, process-intensive work and long tasks that could be automated. To tackle these problems, the company evaluated its agentic coworkers against real enterprise use cases, giving organizations a faster way to deploy AI workers without developing or validating them from scratch.

The initial lineup of coworkers includes an enterprise operations AI coworker, along with a CloudOps engineer, AccessOps manager, SecOps manager and DeviceOps manager. These AI coworkers can work across enterprise systems including AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, Okta, Active Directory, Splunk and Google SecOps.

The company said every AI Coworker comes out of the box with the skills and integrations needed for its role, reducing the work IT teams would otherwise spend wiring up systems and validating procedures.

Every agent can be quickly tailored to internal infrastructure, company culture, specialized expertise and business logic. Using that, they can quickly generate and tackle large volumes of recurring operational work under the supervision of IT and security teams. The company added that administrators will retain full control of agent management, allowing them to decide what systems an agent can access, what actions it can perform and how those actions are governed.

The objective is not merely to provide a catalog of available agents with a card to explain their capabilities. Atomicwork’s certification verifies that each AI Coworker has the needed integrations and skill coverage for the role to get the work done before deployment.

Atomicwork said customers using access automation have already seen speed-ups, with applications that don’t require approval having a median turnaround of about 18 seconds, while those requiring approval have a turnaround of about 2.5 hours. In contrast, the industry standard, which can be heavily influenced by business maturity and the risk behind the application’s use, could take between a full day and three business days depending on the amount of automation behind the scenes.

The company said this marketplace represents the beginning of a broader plan to create an ecosystem of enterprise AI Coworkers, built and certified by Atomicwork. Third parties will also be able to contribute skills and integrations through its Model Context Protocol store and skill registry to enhance coworker capabilities.

“This launch is the first step toward a third-party AI Coworker marketplace, where partners publish their own coworkers and certify them against our enterprise bench,” said Rayapati.
